title: Hasidism for everyone
hookLine: Buber, Heschel and Zalman Schachter-Shalomi brought Hasidic ideas to wide audiences
last: WOMEN, TOO, TAUGHT AND HELD THE COURTS.

cards: Rabbi Zusya lies on his deathbed, and he's afraid. His students are puzzled. You, afraid?
He answers with a story about himself. When I come before the heavenly court, he says, they won't ask me, Zusya, why weren't you Moses? They'll ask me, Zusya, why weren't you Zusya?
That little tale was told among Hasidim. Then it traveled. It turns up in sermons, classrooms and graduation speeches, far from any rebbe's table.

teach.b: Hasidism for everyone. Three teachers carried Hasidic ideas beyond the court. First, Martin Buber.

He gathered Hasidic tales from old Hebrew and Yiddish books and retold them in German, and from there they reached English. Through him, readers who would never visit a court met Zusya and the Baal Shem Tov.
Buber heard in Hasidism a teaching that God is met in the ordinary meeting between people, here, now, not somewhere far away. Second, Abraham Joshua Heschel.
He came from a family of Hasidic rebbes and became a teacher and writer in America.
In his book on the Sabbath, he describes Shabbat as holiness in time rather than in a place, a sanctuary built of hours. He wrote about wonder, and about a God who cares about human beings.

Third, Zalman Schachter-Shalomi, usually called Reb Zalman. He was trained in Chabad, then helped found what became Jewish Renewal, bringing niggunim, Hasidic stories and meditative prayer into new communities.

Not everyone was pleased. Some critics, including the scholar Gershom Scholem, said Buber picked out the tales, set aside the Hasidic teachers' own written teachings, and read his own philosophy into what was left.
Some Hasidim would say the court, its law and its life, is the point. Others answer that the sparks were always meant to travel. You don't have to settle it.
Notice only that Zusya's question now gets asked in rooms where no one wears a shtreimel.

how: Readers meet Hasidic ideas through Buber's retold tales and Heschel's books, and in Jewish Renewal and other communities that sing niggunim and tell Hasidic stories; Hasidic courts continue their own life of study and prayer.

games.q: you are Martin Buber, holding old Hebrew and Yiddish books of Hasidic tales. what do you do with them?
o: retell them in German for wide readers.
write new tales of your own instead.
games.why: Buber retold them, and readers who would never visit a court met Zusya and the Baal Shem Tov. not everyone liked the result.

practice: Let Zusya's question come to you in your own name: not why weren't you someone braver or holier or more well-known, just why weren't you you? Is there one part of yourself you've been setting aside to look like someone else?
Don't scold yourself; just notice it and breathe with it, and if you pray, hold the question there.

wordCard.voice: Hasidism for everyone. Buber, Heschel and Reb Zalman carried Hasidic tales and ideas to wide audiences, and people still argue about what traveled and what stayed behind. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: Hasidism, the teaching and way of life of the Hasidim.
